title: Postgres and Supabase superpowers
summary: How Supabase builds auth, file storage, live updates, AI search and server logic around one Postgres database, and the one rule that keeps it all safe.
youWillLearn: How Supabase Auth and Storage keep their data in your Postgres database, and Realtime streams its changes
How to link your own tables to auth.users with a profiles table
How pgvector lets Notely search notes by meaning
When to use a Postgres function, and when an Edge Function
Why row level security is the price of all this power

glossary.Supabase: A hosted platform built around one Postgres database, adding auth, file storage, realtime updates, an API and serverless functions.
glossary.Postgres schema: A named folder of tables inside one Postgres database, like auth, storage or public.
glossary.auth.users: The table where Supabase Auth keeps one row per account. Managed by Supabase; you link to it, you do not edit it.
glossary.bucket: A named container for files in Supabase Storage, like a top-level folder with its own access rules.
glossary.Realtime: The Supabase service that pushes database changes and messages to connected browsers as they happen.
glossary.extension: An add-on that gives Postgres new types and functions, switched on with create extension.
glossary.pgvector: A Postgres extension that adds a vector column type and fast search for the closest vectors.
glossary.embedding: A long list of numbers an AI model produces from a text, placed so that texts with similar meaning get similar numbers.
glossary.RPC: Remote procedure call: the app calls a named function on the server, here a Postgres function, through supabase.rpc().
glossary.Edge Function: A small TypeScript function Supabase runs on its servers, outside the database, for things like calling a paid API with a secret key.
glossary.RLS: Row level security: Postgres rules that decide, row by row, which rows each user may read or change.
glossary.service role key: A Supabase server key (newer projects call it the secret key) with full access that skips row level security. For trusted server code only.

steps.title: Four features, four services?
body: Maya's wish list for Notely: sign in with email, attach photos to notes, see edits from her other devices live, and ask the AI "find my notes about Lisbon".
The obvious plan is four services: an auth provider, a file host, a realtime server, a vector database. Four bills, four dashboards, and four copies of "who is Maya" to keep in sync.

scene.caption: Four separate services, each with its own idea of who Maya is.

steps.title: One Postgres, with services around it
body: Supabase takes a different route: one Postgres database in the middle, with services wrapped around it. Auth and Storage keep their data in tables of that same database, and Realtime listens to its changes.
So "who is Maya" lives in one place, and one set of rules, written in SQL, can protect all of it.

callout.text: A house with one fuse box. Lights, oven and heating are separate rooms, but the wiring meets in one place, and one switch can cut them all.

scene.caption: Every service is built on the same Postgres database.

steps.title: Auth: your users are rows in a table
body: When Maya signs up, Supabase Auth adds a row to auth.users, in a separate schema called auth. Do not edit that table yourself.
Your own user data goes in a profiles table whose primary key is also a foreign key to auth.users. Inside SQL, auth.uid() returns the id of whoever is making the request.

code.caption: From here on, Notely's user ids are uuids from auth.users, not the small numbers of lesson 1.

scene.caption: Sign-in writes to auth.users. Notely's profiles table points at it.

steps.title: Storage: files outside, facts inside
body: Photos do not belong in table rows. Supabase Storage keeps files in buckets, and records each file's path and owner in storage.objects, a regular Postgres table.
Your notes table stores only the file path. Who may upload or read a file is decided by policies on storage.objects, in the same SQL as everything else.

code.caption: Starting the path with the user's id makes "only your own folder" policies easy to write.

scene.caption: The photo goes to a bucket. Its path and owner become a row in Postgres.

steps.title: Realtime: the table taps you on the shoulder
body: Realtime lets the browser subscribe to changes. When Maya adds a note on her phone, her laptop hears about it within moments and updates the list.
You switch it on per table, then subscribe in the client. Realtime checks your security rules, so Maya only hears about rows she is allowed to read.

code.caption: First, in a migration: alter publication supabase_realtime add table notes;

scene.caption: A new row in notes is pushed to every open Notely tab that may see it.

steps.title: pgvector: search by meaning
body: pgvector is a Postgres extension that adds a vector column type. An AI model turns each note into an embedding: a long list of numbers that captures its meaning.
Store it next to the note. To search, embed the question, then sort notes by distance. "Trips to Portugal" finds the Lisbon note, though no word matches.

code.caption: The number in vector(1024) must match your embedding model's output size.

callout.text: Your notes and their embeddings live in one database, so one query can filter by owner, skip deleted notes and rank by meaning. This is the retrieval half of RAG, which you will use in the AI module.

scene.caption: The question becomes a vector. Postgres returns the closest notes.

steps.title: Functions: SQL the app can call by name
body: A Postgres function packs SQL into a named command. Notely wraps the search in match_notes, and the app calls it with supabase.rpc(), an RPC.

An Edge Function is different: TypeScript on Supabase's servers, outside the database. Like a Next.js API route, it can hold secrets and call outside APIs such as Claude. Use Postgres functions for data work.

code.code:
create function match_notes(query vector(1024), n int)
returns setof notes
language sql stable
as $$
  select * from notes
  where deleted_at is null
  order by embedding <=> query
  limit n;
$$;

-- from Next.js:
-- supabase.rpc('match_notes', { query: embedding, n: 5 })
code.caption: It runs as the caller by default, so RLS still limits it to Maya's own notes.

scene.caption: The app calls one named function. It runs the search inside Postgres.

steps.title: Superpowers need row level security
body: Tables in the public schema are normally reachable from the browser through Supabase's API, with your project's public key. Without RLS, anyone who opens dev tools can read every note.
Turn RLS on for every public table and write a policy for each action. Keep the service role key on the server only: it skips RLS entirely.

callout.text: Ask Claude Code to list every table and whether RLS is on, then read each policy: does it compare to auth.uid()? Is the service role key only in server code, never behind NEXT_PUBLIC_? Is every security definer function intended? Supabase's Security Advisor flags many of these.

scene.caption: Without RLS, the public key opens every row to anyone.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Supabase is one Postgres database with services around it. Auth users and file records are rows in it, and Realtime streams its changes. pgvector adds search by meaning, Postgres functions run data logic by name, and Edge Functions handle secrets outside the database.
One database means one set of rules: turn on RLS everywhere.

scene.caption: With RLS on, the public key only ever reaches the rows a policy allows.

quiz.question: Notely needs each user's display name and avatar path. Where should they live?

options.why: Supabase Auth manages that table. Changing it yourself can break sign-in and future updates.
Your data stays in your own table, one-to-one with each account, protected by your own RLS policies.
It lives on one device only, so Maya's phone would never see what she set on her laptop.

quiz.question: Maya types "trips to Portugal" and wants her Lisbon note back, though neither word appears in it. Which piece do you reach for?

options.why: Realtime pushes changes as they happen. It does not search anything.
That matches letters, not meaning. The Lisbon note never says Portugal, so it is not found.
Embeddings place similar meanings close together, so the question lands near the Lisbon note even with no shared words.

quiz.question: Saving a note fails with new row violates row-level security policy for table "notes". Claude Code suggests exposing the service role key as NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY. What do you do?

options.text: Refuse. Keep the key server-only, rotate it if it leaked, and write the missing RLS policy.
options.why: The error means no policy allows this insert. A NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable ships to every browser, and that key skips RLS for anyone who finds it.

options.text: Accept, but only for the production deploy.
options.why: Production is exactly where a public, all-powerful key does the most damage.

options.text: Turn RLS off on notes so the error goes away.
options.why: Then the public key can read every user's notes. The error was RLS doing its job.

takeaways: Supabase is one Postgres database with services around it. Auth and Storage keep their data in it; Realtime streams its changes.
Link your own user data to auth.users through a profiles table. Never edit auth.users directly.
pgvector stores embeddings next to your rows, so one query can filter by owner and rank by meaning.
Postgres functions (rpc) for data work, Edge Functions for secrets and outside APIs.
Turn on RLS for every public table, and keep the service role key out of the browser.
